interview_metadata.name: Evan Buscetta
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) — Full 109 questions

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: I was born and raised around Van Buren, Arkansas, in a family that was half Italian-American Sunday dinner and half Arkansas front-porch hospitality. My dad worked with his hands, and my mom did steady office and church volunteer work, so I grew up around people who showed up, brought food, fixed what was broken, and did not make a big show of it. We went to a local Roman Catholic parish, and holidays meant a crowded table, tomato sauce, cornbread, somebody playing music, and cousins running everywhere. I finished high school here. I was never much for college, but I was always the guy who could organize people, talk in front of a room, and keep a list straight. I got married in my twenties, and my wife has been my steady person through every season. Over the years I worked different local jobs and helped with church suppers, theater sets, garden days, and arts events. These days I do not have a paid occupation, but I spend a lot of time volunteering with the Van Buren Arts Council, painting watercolor landscapes, gardening, hiking, and helping coordinate workshops. Anxiety has been part of my life too, and sometimes it gets me wound up, but art, hiking, prayer, and my wife help keep me grounded.

follow_ups.question: What are some childhood memories that still feel vivid to you?
follow_ups.response: My grandma stirring red sauce on Sunday, my dad showing me how to square a board, and walking out of church into hot Arkansas sun all stick with me. I also remember drawing hills and barns on notebook paper when I should have been doing math.

follow_ups.question: When did art become more than just a casual interest?
follow_ups.response: Probably in my late thirties. I started painting Arkansas River scenes and Ozark ridges in watercolor, and people at church and the arts council took me seriously enough that I started taking myself seriously too.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: One big crossroads came when I stopped trying to measure myself only by paid work. I had gone through a stretch where steady work was hard, partly because of anxiety and partly because I did not know where I fit. I could have withdrawn and felt embarrassed, but a friend at the arts council asked me to help coordinate a volunteer watercolor workshop. I made sign-up sheets, priced supplies, called people, handled a disagreement over booth space, and by the end everybody said, 'Evan, you ought to do more of this.' That changed how I saw myself. I realized I could be useful without having a formal title.

follow_ups.question: Who was the friend who pulled you into that first workshop?
follow_ups.response: A local painter named Mary Grant. She is not famous, but around here she is one of those people everybody trusts with art things.

follow_ups.question: What did that change in your week after that?
follow_ups.response: I started going to arts council meetings twice a month, keeping a binder of budgets and contacts, and saying yes to more public speaking than I ever expected.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it 'just happened'. What about you?
transcript.response: It was both. Mary asking me just happened, but deciding not to hide behind embarrassment was a conscious choice.

follow_ups.question: What made you say yes?
follow_ups.response: My wife said, 'You are good at this, and people need you.' That mattered.

follow_ups.question: Did it feel risky?
follow_ups.response: Yes, mostly because I worried I would mess it up in public.

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: Yes. A little more guidance about anxiety and work transitions would have helped. I think churches, clinics, and community groups could do better at connecting people to practical support without making them feel ashamed.

follow_ups.question: What kind of help would have mattered most?
follow_ups.response: Someone sitting down with me to make a plan, not just handing me a pamphlet.

follow_ups.question: Is that part of why Mental Health First Aid interests you?
follow_ups.response: Exactly. I want to be that calm first person for somebody else.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: I am married, and my wife is the most important person in my daily life. We do not have children at home. We built a good rhythm together: coffee in the morning, supper most nights, church some Sundays, music or theater when we can afford it. My extended family still matters too. I have cousins nearby, and we see them at holidays, cookouts, parish events, and sometimes Razorbacks games on TV. My wife is patient with my anxious spells, but she also does not let me disappear into them. She will send me outside to water tomatoes or tell me to go walk the river trail.

follow_ups.question: What do you and your wife usually do together for fun?
follow_ups.response: We go to bluegrass or folk shows when they come through, watch community theater, cook ribs on weekends, and take short day trips.

follow_ups.question: Do you have children who live elsewhere?
follow_ups.response: No, we do not have children. We have nieces, nephews, and younger folks from church and the arts council we care about.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: My parents are still a big part of how I think about family, though they are older now. I also have siblings and cousins I stay in touch with, mostly by phone, Sunday visits, and family meals.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see extended family?
follow_ups.response: Usually monthly, more around holidays.

follow_ups.question: Are those relationships close?
follow_ups.response: Close enough that people call when something breaks or when food is ready.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: My friends are mostly connected through the arts council, community theater, church, hiking, and the garden. Mary Grant is a good art friend. I also have a few men from the Ozark Trail Hiking Club I see most Saturdays, and we know each other's knees, boots, and snack preferences by now. In theater, I help backstage and sometimes act, so there are people I may not see every week but trust quickly when a production is running.

follow_ups.question: Who do you see most often outside family?
follow_ups.response: The hiking group on Saturdays and the arts council folks during workshop weeks.

follow_ups.question: How do you keep in touch?
follow_ups.response: Mostly text threads, Facebook groups, phone calls, and seeing each other in person.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: We live in Van Buren, not far from the river and old downtown. It is the kind of place where you recognize trucks before you recognize faces. There are older homes, church signs, yards with tomatoes or bird feeders, and people who will wave even if they are in a hurry. I like being near the Arkansas River and close enough to Fort Smith for errands but still in a smaller community. The downtown has history and charm, and the arts crowd is small but real.

follow_ups.question: Where do you spend time nearby?
follow_ups.response: The river area, the garden, downtown art spaces, church, and local diners.

follow_ups.question: Do neighbors know each other?
follow_ups.response: Yes, at least on our street. People notice if your car has not moved.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: I feel mostly safe. We lock doors and keep porch lights on, but I am comfortable walking in the evening and working in the yard.

follow_ups.question: Has anything happened that made you feel unsafe?
follow_ups.response: A few car break-ins nearby, nothing violent close to us.

follow_ups.question: Do you know who to call for help?
follow_ups.response: Yes, neighbors first for small things, police or fire for emergencies.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: The good is the community, the river, and the slower pace. The hard part is limited jobs, limited health care choices, and sometimes everybody knowing your business.

follow_ups.question: Would you move?
follow_ups.response: Not unless we had to. Van Buren feels like home.

follow_ups.question: What would you improve?
follow_ups.response: More arts funding, better mental health services, and more sidewalks.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: It is just me and my wife in the house. We share the routines pretty naturally. I cook a lot, tend the garden, fix small things, and handle some volunteer paperwork at the kitchen table. She helps keep our calendar sane and is better than I am at saying no when we are overcommitted.

follow_ups.question: Do you have pets?
follow_ups.response: No pets right now.

follow_ups.question: What rooms get used most?
follow_ups.response: Kitchen, porch, and the spare room I use for painting and supplies.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: Everyone is permanent. It is just the two of us.

follow_ups.question: Any short-term guests now?
follow_ups.response: No.

follow_ups.question: Any expected soon?
follow_ups.response: No, not right now.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that
transcript.response: Sometimes a niece or cousin stays one night during holidays, but nobody regularly.

follow_ups.question: How often does that happen?
follow_ups.response: A few times a year.

follow_ups.question: Where do they stay?
follow_ups.response: On the foldout in the spare room.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No, nobody.

follow_ups.question: No one away at school?
follow_ups.response: No.

follow_ups.question: No one hospitalized?
follow_ups.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: Most weekdays I get up around 6:30 or 7, make coffee, check messages, and water the garden if it is warm. Mondays and Wednesdays often have arts council planning or calls. Tuesdays I may paint in the morning and do errands in Fort Smith. Thursdays are good for theater or workshop prep. Fridays we keep lighter if we can. Saturdays I often hike with the Ozark Trail Hiking Club or help at the community garden. Sundays are church, family food, or a quiet afternoon.

follow_ups.question: When do you usually paint?
follow_ups.response: Mornings, especially after coffee and before the day gets noisy.

follow_ups.question: What is your busiest recurring commitment?
follow_ups.response: Arts workshops when one is coming up. Those weeks can take over.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: I do not have a paid job right now. I do unpaid volunteer work that looks a lot like work: coordinating volunteers, setting up art displays, managing small budgets, making calls, and speaking at community events. The timing changes, but I probably spend ten to fifteen hours in a normal week on arts council or community projects, more before an exhibit or workshop.

follow_ups.question: Are you looking for paid work?
follow_ups.response: I would like a part-time volunteer coordinator role if the right one opens up.

follow_ups.question: Why part-time?
follow_ups.response: It fits my energy, anxiety, and family rhythm better than full-time work.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: I handle a lot of cooking, grocery planning, basic repairs, and garden work. I also keep first-aid supplies for events and try to check on a couple older folks from church. I am the person people call when they need folding tables, a sign-up list, or somebody to smooth over a disagreement.

follow_ups.question: How often do you cook?
follow_ups.response: Most nights, with bigger meals on weekends.

follow_ups.question: What do people ask you for most?
follow_ups.response: Planning help, setup help, and calm talking when tempers rise.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: I have been trying to make my routine steadier because anxiety gets worse when days are too loose. I started blocking mornings for painting or walking, afternoons for errands and volunteer calls, and evenings for home. I also began looking into Mental Health First Aid certification, so I have been reading about class options and peer support.

follow_ups.question: Has the new structure helped?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially having a morning walk or garden task.

follow_ups.question: What still disrupts it?
follow_ups.response: Last-minute event needs and my own tendency to overcommit.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: We do not have children, so there is no school routine in our household. I do pay attention to school calendars because arts workshops and theater events often involve families, students, or teachers.

follow_ups.question: Do you work with kids through art events?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes, yes, usually supervised workshops or family art days.

follow_ups.question: What do kids seem to enjoy?
follow_ups.response: Hands-on painting, messy craft stations, and anything they can take home.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: My experiences have mostly been ordinary. Traffic stops, seeing officers at community events, and calling once when a neighbor's shed looked broken into. I have not personally had a major bad experience, but I know not everyone is treated the same, and I try to keep that in mind.

follow_ups.question: How were your traffic stops?
follow_ups.response: Routine. Nervous, but routine.

follow_ups.question: Do police come to local events?
follow_ups.response: Yes, for traffic, parades, and safety at larger gatherings.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: One officer helped direct cars during an arts event when our volunteer parking plan fell apart. That was a good experience because he was patient with us.

follow_ups.question: Did that change how you planned events?
follow_ups.response: Yes, now I ask about parking and safety earlier.

follow_ups.question: Any negative examples?
follow_ups.response: Nothing personal beyond hearing friends describe tense stops.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: I have never been arrested. I know a couple people who had DUIs years back, but no close family member is currently dealing with arrest or jail.

follow_ups.question: Did those DUIs affect your view of alcohol?
follow_ups.response: They made me cautious about driving after any drinking.

follow_ups.question: Was your family affected directly?
follow_ups.response: No, not directly.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: I vote most of the time, especially presidential, governor, local tax issues, and school board races when I know enough. I have missed smaller elections, usually because I did not pay attention soon enough. I see voting as part of being a community member, like showing up to a meeting.

follow_ups.question: Do you vote early or on Election Day?
follow_ups.response: Usually early if I am organized, Election Day if not.

follow_ups.question: Do you discuss votes with your wife?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially local issues.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: I would call myself an Independent who leans moderate, maybe a little more Democratic on health care, mental health, arts funding, and how people on the margins are treated. At the same time, I grew up in a place where people value faith, family, personal responsibility, and not wasting money, and those values are real to me too. I do not like politics that turns neighbors into enemies. I care about local issues: parks, schools, libraries, downtown businesses, river access, and whether people can get medical care without going broke. On national politics, I get frustrated with the shouting. I want practical leaders who tell the truth and remember small towns.

follow_ups.question: Are there issues that decide your vote?
follow_ups.response: Health care, mental health access, local investment, and basic decency matter a lot.

follow_ups.question: Do you feel represented by either party?
follow_ups.response: Only partly. Both parties lose me when they act like regular people are props.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: I have become more outspoken about mental health and health care. Ten or fifteen years ago I might have thought people just needed to tough it out more. Living with anxiety and seeing friends struggle changed that. I also care more now about public funding for the arts and community programs because I have seen how little money can create a real place for people to belong.

follow_ups.question: What changed your mind most?
follow_ups.response: Personal experience and watching people I respect struggle quietly.

follow_ups.question: Have you changed parties?
follow_ups.response: No, I have mostly stayed Independent.

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: They have affected me somewhat. I am a white man in Arkansas, so I know I have not lived those experiences. But listening to Black artists, neighbors, and people online made me think harder about policing, opportunity, and whose stories get believed. It has not made me join a protest, but it has made me listen more carefully.

follow_ups.question: Where did you hear those perspectives?
follow_ups.response: Some through Facebook, some through arts circles, and some through interviews and local conversations.

follow_ups.question: Was there conflict in those conversations?
follow_ups.response: Yes, sometimes people got defensive fast.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: I think the basic issue is whether people are treated with equal dignity and whether institutions admit when patterns are unfair. I also think small towns need ways to talk about race without everybody shutting down. My instinct is to bring it back to listening, accountability, and practical reforms, not slogans only.

follow_ups.question: What practical reforms do you mean?
follow_ups.response: Training, transparency, body cameras used properly, and real complaint processes.

follow_ups.question: Do arts spaces have a role?
follow_ups.response: Yes. Art can let people tell stories that meetings cannot hold well.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: I think we are still carrying history in our schools, neighborhoods, churches, and hiring. I do not think guilt alone helps, but honesty does. In community arts, I have been trying to notice whose work gets shown and who feels welcome in the room.

follow_ups.question: Have you changed anything in your organizing?
follow_ups.response: I try to invite a wider range of artists and not rely only on the same circle.

follow_ups.question: Do people respond well?
follow_ups.response: Mostly, though some folks ask why it matters.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: I have talked with family and friends and tried to keep my ears open. I have not joined protests, but I have pushed back gently when someone says racism is all in the past.

follow_ups.question: Where do those conversations happen?
follow_ups.response: Family meals, Facebook, church parking lots, and arts meetings.

follow_ups.question: How do you push back?
follow_ups.response: I ask questions and bring up examples instead of yelling.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: It is mixed. My wife is thoughtful and probably pushes me to be more open. Some cousins think the conversation goes too far. Arts friends are more likely to talk about inclusion and representation. Hiking friends usually avoid politics unless somebody else brings it up.

follow_ups.question: Has it strained relationships?
follow_ups.response: A little, but not broken any close ones.

follow_ups.question: Who influences you most?
follow_ups.response: My wife and arts friends who have different life experiences.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: Overall I would say fair to good. I am active: I hike, garden, and move around at events. I carry some extra weight, and comfort food can get away from me. Anxiety is the main health issue I manage. Physically I get normal middle-aged aches, mostly knees and back after hikes or hauling tables.

follow_ups.question: Do you have a regular doctor?
follow_ups.response: Yes, a primary care clinic locally.

follow_ups.question: What helps most day to day?
follow_ups.response: Walking, gardening, sleep, and not overloading the calendar.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: It is easy when the weather is good and I have hiking or gardening built into the week. It is hard when I am anxious, because then I want fried catfish, extra bacon, or a second helping of ribs and cornbread. Money and appointment availability can also make health care feel like a chore.

follow_ups.question: What healthy habit is most reliable?
follow_ups.response: Saturday hikes and watering the garden.

follow_ups.question: What food is hardest to moderate?
follow_ups.response: Fried catfish and bacon, no question.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: No major diagnosis or broken bones in the last two years. I did have a spell where anxiety and sleep got worse, and I talked with my doctor about it. I have had knee soreness after longer hikes, so I have been more careful about stretching and not pretending I am twenty-five.

follow_ups.question: Did you change treatment for anxiety?
follow_ups.response: Mostly routines and check-ins; no major medication change recently.

follow_ups.question: Do knee issues limit hiking?
follow_ups.response: Only on steep trails. I use poles when needed.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: Anxiety has affected my ability to take on full-time paid work. It does not stop me from being useful, but I have to manage commitments carefully.

follow_ups.question: What happens when you overcommit?
follow_ups.response: I sleep poorly, eat badly, and get irritable.

follow_ups.question: How do you prevent that?
follow_ups.response: My wife and I review the calendar before I say yes.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, it's not your health problem, but the health of a loved one. Has this been an issue for you?
transcript.response: Yes, mostly with aging parents and older church friends. There are appointments, falls, medication questions, and the emotional strain of watching people slow down. I am not a full-time caregiver, but I help with rides, meals, and checking in.

follow_ups.question: Who do you help most often?
follow_ups.response: Older relatives and a couple parish members.

follow_ups.question: How often?
follow_ups.response: A few times a month, more if someone has an appointment.

transcript.question_text: Tell me what it has been like trying to get the health care you or your immediate family need. Have you ever had to forgo getting the health care you need?
transcript.response: We have usually gotten care, but it can be slow and expensive enough that you think twice. Specialist appointments can mean driving and waiting. I have delayed dental work and put off counseling at times because of cost. We try not to skip necessary care, but we do stretch things.

follow_ups.question: What care is hardest to access?
follow_ups.response: Mental health counseling and dental.

follow_ups.question: Do you have insurance?
follow_ups.response: Yes through the household, but deductibles and copays still matter.

transcript.question_text: Have you or your immediate family ever used alternative forms of medicine? This might include indigenous, non-western, or informal forms of care.
transcript.response: Nothing formal like that. We use home remedies sometimes: herbal tea, hot baths, stretching, prayer, and old family food when someone is sick. I respect doctors, but I also believe comfort and routine help a person heal.

follow_ups.question: Any family remedies?
follow_ups.response: Chicken soup, garlic, honey tea, and being told to rest whether you want to or not.

follow_ups.question: Do you use supplements?
follow_ups.response: Only basic vitamins occasionally.

transcript.question_text: During tough times, some people tell us they cope by smoking or drinking. How about for you?
transcript.response: I do not smoke. I drink occasionally, maybe a beer at a cookout or a glass of wine with dinner, but I do not use alcohol as my main coping tool. My unhealthy coping is more likely food, staying up late, or getting too wrapped up in a project.

follow_ups.question: How often do you drink?
follow_ups.response: A few times a month, sometimes less.

follow_ups.question: What do you reach for under stress?
follow_ups.response: Comfort food and busywork.

transcript.question_text: Other people say they cope by relying on prescriptions, pain medications, marijuana, or other substances. How about for you and can you describe your most recent experience of using them, if any?
transcript.response: I do not use marijuana or other drugs. I take over-the-counter pain medicine after a hard hike or when my back complains. I have talked with my doctor about anxiety, but I am cautious with prescriptions and follow medical advice. My most recent pain medicine use was ibuprofen after a Saturday hike.

follow_ups.question: Any concerns about medications?
follow_ups.response: I want to avoid depending on anything without a clear need.

follow_ups.question: Do you keep medication at home?
follow_ups.response: Basic first-aid and over-the-counter medicine.

transcript.question_text: How are you and your family coping with, or paying for, your health care needs right now?
transcript.response: We budget for copays and prescriptions as best we can. We use insurance, compare costs when possible, and sometimes delay non-urgent things until we have room. My wife is more organized with paperwork, and I keep receipts in a folder because medical bills can get confusing.

follow_ups.question: Do medical costs cause stress?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially dental or anything unexpected.

follow_ups.question: Who handles bills?
follow_ups.response: We both do, but my wife is better with deadlines.

transcript.question_text: Some people are excited about medical vaccination, and others, not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: I am generally pro-vaccine. I get routine shots and think vaccines are part of taking care of the community, especially older folks.

follow_ups.question: Did you get COVID vaccines?
follow_ups.response: Yes.

follow_ups.question: Any hesitation?
follow_ups.response: Normal questions at first, but I trusted my doctor.

transcript.question_text: What are your trusted sources of information about the vaccine?
transcript.response: My primary care doctor is first. I also trust the CDC, the Arkansas Department of Health, and pharmacists I know locally. I do not take medical advice from random Facebook posts, though I see plenty of them.

follow_ups.question: Do you discuss vaccines at church or family gatherings?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes, but I try not to argue.

follow_ups.question: Who is most persuasive to you?
follow_ups.response: A doctor who knows my history.

transcript.question_text: Now we're going to talk a bit more about what life was like for you over the past year. Tell me all about how you have been feeling.
transcript.response: This past year has been a mix of gratitude and worry. I have felt useful with arts council work, especially when a workshop goes well. But I also get anxious about money, health, and whether I am doing enough. Some mornings I wake up with my mind already making lists. Painting, hiking, prayer, and talking with my wife help me come back down.

follow_ups.question: When is anxiety worst?
follow_ups.response: Early morning or the night before a big event.

follow_ups.question: What does a good day feel like?
follow_ups.response: Coffee, a walk, useful work, supper with my wife, and no racing thoughts.

transcript.question_text: Tell me a story about a time in the last year when you were in a rough place or struggling emotionally.
transcript.response: Before one arts display, two volunteers argued over whose work should be featured, and I took it too personally. I went home feeling like I had failed everybody. That night I ate too much, slept badly, and thought about quitting. The next morning my wife told me to call both people and deal with the facts. I did, and it settled down, but it reminded me how fast anxiety can turn a small conflict into a disaster in my head.

follow_ups.question: What did you say on the calls?
follow_ups.response: I listened first, then set clearer display rules and time slots.

follow_ups.question: Did you quit?
follow_ups.response: No, but I did write down better guidelines.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they struggle with depression, anxiety, or something else like that. How about for you?
transcript.response: Anxiety, yes. Depression not in a diagnosed way, though I can get low when anxiety wears me out. I have learned that I need structure, exercise, art, and honest conversation. That is part of why Mental Health First Aid appeals to me.

follow_ups.question: Have you been diagnosed with anxiety?
follow_ups.response: Yes, I have discussed anxiety with my doctor and recognize it as a real condition.

follow_ups.question: What warning signs do you notice?
follow_ups.response: Tight chest, racing lists, irritability, and wanting to cancel everything.

transcript.question_text: How has it been for your family?
transcript.response: My wife has had to learn my patterns, and that is not always fair to her. Family is supportive, though some relatives still think anxiety is just worry.

follow_ups.question: Does your wife have support too?
follow_ups.response: Yes, friends and family, and she is honest with me when she needs space.

follow_ups.question: Do relatives talk openly about mental health?
follow_ups.response: More than they used to, but not easily.

transcript.question_text: Some people say that religion or spirituality is important in their lives, for others not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: Religion is important to me, though I am not perfect about attendance. I was raised Roman Catholic, and I still identify Catholic. summaries.demographer: Evan Buscetta is a 49-year-old married White non-Hispanic man living with his wife in Van Buren, Arkansas (Q51, Q84, Q88, Q89). He was born in Fort Smith, grew up in Van Buren, completed high school, and is not currently enrolled in school or employed for pay (Q85-Q91, Q65-Q73). His household owns a modest mortgaged home and relies mainly on his wife's income, with a tight but functioning budget (Q58, Q74, Q83). His life-course profile reflects local rootedness, stable marriage, no children, strong extended family ties, and middle-to-lower-middle financial caution (Q05, Q06, Q63, Q82).
summaries.behavioral_economist: Evan shows strong prosocial motivation and identity utility from unpaid community work, even without direct wages (Q16, Q65, Q83). His choices are shaped by loss aversion around medical bills, car repairs, and debt, leading to pantry meals, delayed trips, and careful budgeting when expenses rise (Q60-Q64, Q81-Q82). He has present-biased comfort coping under anxiety, especially overeating fried or rich foods, but offsets that with routines such as hiking, gardening, and calendar structure (Q32, Q38, Q50). He is cautious with risk, preferring part-time work, modest savings, and practical local commitments over large uncertain changes (Q16, Q61, Q108).
summaries.political_scientist: Evan is a moderate Independent who leans Democratic on health care, mental health, arts funding, and inclusion, while retaining culturally conservative values around faith, family, responsibility, and budgeting (Q24, Q95, Q96). He votes most of the time and treats voting as part of local civic responsibility (Q23). His institutional trust is selective: he trusts doctors and public health sources for vaccines, values local community institutions, and is wary of national political polarization (Q24, Q42). On race and policing, he is sympathetic but cautious, preferring listening, local inclusion, and practical reforms over protest participation (Q26-Q30).
summaries.psychologist: Evan presents as conscientious, socially warm, community-oriented, and creative, with a strong need to be useful and dependable (Q01, Q16, Q109). Anxiety is his main mental health challenge, expressed through racing thoughts, sleep disruption, overcommitment, irritability, and comfort eating (Q43-Q45). He regulates emotion through structure, watercolor painting, hiking, gardening, prayer, cooking, and support from his wife (Q18, Q31, Q43, Q47, Q50). His self-concept is organized around transforming personal anxiety and informal skills into service, especially through arts coordination and future Mental Health First Aid work (Q04, Q45, Q108).
